theory.intro: The diagonals of a kite meet at right angles, and the same is true of a rhombus. A kite fits exactly inside a rectangle built on its two diagonals and fills half of it, so the area is half the product of the diagonals.
facts: **Area $=\dfrac{xy}{2}$**, where $x$ and $y$ are the lengths of the two **diagonals**.
A diagonal joins two **non-adjacent** vertices, so it runs corner to corner across the inside of the shape.
A rhombus is also a kite, so $A=\dfrac{xy}{2}$ works for a rhombus whenever the diagonals are known.
A **side** of a rhombus is not a diagonal, so a side length can never be substituted into this formula.
When a diagonal is split into two parts, add the parts to get the whole diagonal before substituting.
Both diagonals must be in the same unit, and the area is written in square units: mm$^{2}$, cm$^{2}$, m$^{2}$.
steps: Identify the two diagonals $x$ and $y$, adding part lengths where a diagonal is split.
Multiply, halve, and write the answer with squared units.

development.question_text: The diagonals of a rhombus are $18$ cm and $11$ cm long. Find its area, in square centimetres.
A kite has diagonals of length $7.4$ m and $5$ m. Find its area, in square metres.

mastery.solution_text:
The formula $A=\frac{xy}{2}$ needs the two diagonals, which run from corner to corner across the inside of the rhombus.
Here $10$ cm is a side and $8$ cm is the perpendicular height, so neither length is a diagonal and the formula does not apply.

$A_{\text{A}}=\frac{12 \times 9}{2}$
$=\frac{108}{2}$
$=54\text{ cm}^2$
$A_{\text{B}}=\frac{18 \times 6}{2}$
$=\frac{108}{2}$
$=54\text{ cm}^2$
Both kites have an area of $54$ cm$^{2}$, so their areas are equal.

mastery.question_text: One diagonal of a kite is three times as long as the other. The shorter diagonal is $8$ cm long. Find the area of the kite, in square centimetres.
